title: Introduction
text: This study is part of a decades-long international collaboration to learn about the systematics, evolution, and island biogeography of East Asian and Philippine birds. This chapter of that story involves the systematics of a particularly complex group within the white-eye genus Zosterops. The systematics of the white-eyes of East Asia and the Philippines, dubbed the Asiatic white-eyes, has proven to be confounding. Various studies have made strides in understanding this group but have suffered from insufficient sampling (Lim et al. 2018; Jones and Kennedy 2008; Gwee et al. 2020; Oliveros, Andersen, and Moyle 2021; Moyle et al. 2009). We produced a RADseq dataset and coupled those data with a smaller allele-based Sanger sequenced dataset and linear morphometrics from museum study skins. Here we will describe in detail, perhaps excruciating, the methods and analyses in this work. The hope is that the work will be reproducible by our colleagues and accessible for students, especially for those learning to grapple with the complexities of large-scale single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) datasets.

title: Introduction
text:
Sampling
The strength of this study lies in its comprehensive sampling effort. 208 genetic samples and 354 museum skins were analyzed from several museums in the United States, China, Taiwan, and Japan. All of the sampling in this study is accessioned in natural history museums.



An author (HLM) collecting samples on Lanyu Island.


For the Asiatic white-eye complex we have sampled from many populations for the genetic analysis including all but three of the 15 subspecies within the combined Z. japonicus and Z. montanus group. This sampling was geographically widespread ranging from large temperate islands such as Hokkaido and Honshu, tiny, far-flung oceanic islands such as those in the Volcano group in the Pacific, and a variety of tropical islands in the Philippine and Indonesian archipelagos, as well as multiple taxa and populations for continental species ranging from Singapore to the Russian Far East.



An author (BDM) with Zosterops japonicus on the Japanese island of Tsushima.

title: Introduction
text:
Lab work and analysis
All the bench work for this project was conducted either at the University of Kansas for RADseq and Marshall University or Cincinnati Museum Center for the Sanger sequenced loci. Initial analyses were done at the University of Kansas by Devon DeRaad and published in the journal Biological Invasions (DeRaad et al. 2024). Where those initial analyses focused on using the RADseq data and ecological niche modeling to study the origin and spread of the introduced populations in Hawaii and Southern California, this study takes those data and adds Sanger sequences and morphology to focus on the systematics of the group in Asia. The initial basic filtering and preparation of the RADseq data for analysis is documented in (DeRaad et al. 2024). All the analyses here are directed toward solving the puzzle of the species limits within this group and determining their relationships. The lead on those analyses were done by Herman Mays Jr. at Marshall University with considerable help from Laura Kubatko at Ohio State University.



A view of lab work in the lab of one of the authors (HLM) at Marshall University.

title: Introduction
text:
Museum morphometrics
Species are more than just the accumulation of neutral genetic differences. We added phenotypic data to these analyses to make for a more inclusive and integrative investigation of species limits and evolution in this group. Phenotypes in this study were focused on linear morphometrics derived from museum skins. Access to museum collections was generously provided by the American Museum of Natural History, Cincinnati Museum Center, The Field Museum, and the National Museum of Natural History at the Smithsonian. We have immense gratitude for these institutions and their staff for maintaining these collections and making them accessible.



Specimens of Zosterops nigrorum catarmanensis (top) and Z. montanus at the Field Museum, Chicago, IL.

title: Sampling Maps
text:
Getting started
We are using R version 4.5.2, RStudio version 2026.5.1.225 for the analysis. Quarto version 1.6.39 was used to document the workflow.

title: Sampling Maps
text:
General methods summary
Sampling included specimen vouchered tissue samples and museum archived blood sampling from individual banded birds in the field. Samples were sourced from the American Museum of Natural History (New York, NY, USA), Cincinnati Museum Center (Cincinnati, OH, USA), Field Museum of Natural History (Chicago, IL, USA), Institute of Zoology of the Guangdong Academy of Sciences (Guangzhou, People’s Republic of China), University of Kansas Biodiversity Institute and Natural History Museum (Lawrence, KS, USA), Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County (Los Angeles, CA, USA), National Museum of Nature and Science (Tokyo, Japan), Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History (Washington D.C., USA), and the University of Washington Burke Museum (Seattle, WA, USA). For the sake of clarity, we treat Z. japonicus and Z. montanus according to the former taxonomic arrangement (i.e., as separate species) as we test various species delimitation hypotheses. Our sampling includes multiple individuals within each of five out of the six recognized subspecies for Z. japonicus and seven out of the nine subspecies within Z. montanus, including sampling from all the recognized Z. montanus subspecies within the Philippines. A total of 207 genomic DNA (gDNA) samples were used in this study with 166 represented in the Sanger sequencing dataset, 124 represented in the filtered SNP dataset, and 83 samples overlapping both genetic datasets.
Latitude and longitude were available for most of the vouchered museum specimens and where not available were estimated from the locality description using the BerkeleyMapper 2.0 (https://www.gbif.org/tool/81294/berkeleymapper) georeferencing tool. Maps showing approximate locations of individual samples were created using the R packages ggplot2 (Wickham 2016), maps (Becker, Minka, and Deckmyn. 2024), and sf (Pebesma and Bivand 2023).

title: Sampling Maps
text:
Data files
This analysis requires the following data files.

ZosteropsPOPS4_LatLong.txt A text file of individual samples included in the SNP dataset matched with taxon, locale, and latitude and longitude.
ZosteropsPOPS_SANGER_LatLong.txt A text file of individual samples included in the Sanger sequencing dataset that do not appear in the SNP dataset matched with taxon, locale, and latitude and longitude.


Individual samples and collecting localities: SNPs
A tab delimited text file with the individual sample IDs, taxon designations, the name of the sampling locales (designated by island or province), and latitude and longitude was created to generate maps. To reduce the amount of clutter on the maps subspecies were clustered together in shared geographic groups. Zosterops japonicus subspecies were designated as either Z. japonicus alani for the most remote subspecies in the Ogasawara and Volcano Islands or grouped within a single Z. japonicus designation for all the remaining subspecies. Subspecies for Z. montanus were clustered into three groups including a Palawan group (montanus PALAWAN) consisting of Z. montanus parkesi, a northern Philippine group (montanus NORTH) for those subspecies on Mindoro and Luzon (Z. montanus halconensis amd Z. montanus whiteheadi), and a southern Philippine group (montanus SOUTH) including the remaining Z. montanus subspecies included in the study (Z. montanus diuatae, Z. montanus montanus, Z. montanus pectoralis, Z. montanus vulcani, and an unnamed but suggested subspecies on Panay). Subspecies within the Z. everetti and Z. nigrorum species were lumped together under a single species designation for each in the sampling maps but distinguished in later analyses. Samples from introduced populations in Hawaii and California are included in this list, but they are excluded from the final figure. title: Sampling Maps
text:
Packages
Set the working directory to one where the data files ZosteropsPOPS4_LatLong.txt and ZosteropsPOPS_SANGER_LatLong.txt are accessible. Creating the sampling maps requires the following R packages.

logr (Bosak 2024) Optional if you wish to create a log file for the analysis.
dplyr (Wickham et al. 2026)

title: Sampling Maps
section: Read and edit data: SNP sampling
text:
Read and edit data: SNP sampling
Read the data into a data frame using read.csv and indicate that the fields are tab delimited (sep = "\t") and contain a header row (header = TRUE). First complete this process for the sampling data for the SNP dataset.

# Read tab delimited (sep = "\t") file with latitude and longitude
ZLocations <- read.csv(
  "Data/Location files/ZosteropsPOPS4_LatLong.txt", 
                       sep = "\t", header = TRUE)

Remove the samples from the introduced populations. Those samples are from Los Angeles (Z. simplex) and Hawaii (Z. japonicus) and are included in analyses but will not appear on the sampling maps.

# Remove Los Angeles and Hawaii samples
ZLocations_NATIVE <- ZLocations %>% 
  dplyr::filter(!LOCALE %in% c("LOSANGELES", "HAWAII"))

title: Sampling Maps
section: Count individual samples per taxon: SNP sampling
text:
Count individual samples per taxon: SNP sampling
To illustrate the relative number of individual samples from any particular site we will count the number of samples associated with a unique latitude and longitude. First split the data frame by the TAXON column.

# Split by TAXON
Zlocations_NATIVE_TAXON <- split(ZLocations_NATIVE, 
                                 ZLocations_NATIVE$TAXON)

Using a loop count samples grouped by LAT and LONG columns and save this as a new data frame called sampling.df.

# initialize sampling.df which will be a df of samples grouped by unique lat/long
sampling.df<-data.frame(NULL)
# use a for loop to split the dataframe by species and summarize the number 
# of individuals sampled at each locality for each species
for (i in names(Zlocations_NATIVE_TAXON)){
  samps <- Zlocations_NATIVE_TAXON[[i]] %>% 
    dplyr::group_by(LAT, LONG) %>% 
    dplyr::summarize(count=dplyr::n())
  df <- cbind(rep(i, times=nrow(samps)), samps)
  sampling.df <- as.data.frame(rbind(sampling.df, df))
}

title: Sampling Maps
text:
Create a sampling map

Mapping all samples
Download a world base map.

#make base world map
pac<-map_data("world")

First create a sampling map for all the Zosterops samples in the study (excluding those from introduced populations). Include two lines with the geo_point command. One line will define those points from the SNP sampling data frame (sampling.df) and identify those points as filled circles (pch=21). The next line will define the points using the geo_point command for the additional Sanger sequencing samples (samplingSANGER.df) and identify those points as triangles (pch=24). Because many of the sampling locations are the same for different taxa define position = position_jitter(h=0.5, w=0.5) to offset the points on the map so as they do not perfectly overlap. Also set alpha=0.5 to make the points transparent. This will also help in showing those places where sampled taxa overlap in location.

# plot all native samples
ggplot()+
  geom_polygon(data = pac, aes(x=long, y = lat, group = group), 
               fill="lightgrey", col="black", cex=.1)+
  coord_sf(xlim = c(90, 145), ylim = c(-10, 48)) + 
  geom_point(data = sampling.df, aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, 
                                     fill=Species, size=count), 
             position = position_jitter(h = 0.5, w = 0.5), pch=21, 
             color="black", alpha =0.5, show.legend=TRUE) +
  geom_point(data = samplingSANGER.df, aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, 
                                           fill=Species, size=count), 
             position = position_jitter(h = 0.5, w = 0.5), pch=24, 
             color="black", alpha =0.5, show.legend=TRUE) +
  theme_classic()+
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#E6007E", "#004949", "#DB6D00", 
                             "#D82632", "#290AD8", "#FED439", 
                             "#B66DFF", "#006DDB", "#FA9C88", 
                             "#924900", "#7BA9CB", "#008600"))+
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(3,6))+
  guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 8), order=1, 
                             label.theme = element_text(face = "italic"), 
                             position = "left"),
         linewidth = guide_legend(order = 2))+
  theme(legend.position = "left")

ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.









Save the sampling map as a png file.

# Save the sampling plot
ggsave("ZosteropsSamplingMapALL.png", device = "png", 
       width = 9, height = 6.5, units = "in", dpi = 500)



Mapping Ryukyu Island samples
Because many of the samples were collected on small islands and may appear close together at a large scale, create more geographically focused maps for particular regions with heavy sampling. This may be accomplished by editing the coord_sf command to narrow the latitude and longitude for each map. First create a map that is focused on those samples from the Ryukyu Islands.

# plot all native samples in the Ryukyu Islands
ggplot()+

  geom_point(data = samplingSANGER.df, aes(x = Longitude, y = Latitude, 
                                           fill=Species, size=count), 
             position = position_jitter(h = 0.1, w = 0.1), pch=24, 
             color="black", alpha =0.5, show.legend=FALSE) +

  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#E6007E", "#004949", "#DB6D00", 
                             "#D82632", "#290AD8", "#FED439", 
                             "#B66DFF", "#006DDB", "#FA9C88", 
                             "#924900", "#7BA9CB", "#008600"))+
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(3,6))








Save the Ryukyu Islands sampling map as a png file.

# Save the sampling plot
ggsave("ZosteropsSamplingMapRYUKYU.png", device = "png",

title: Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees
text: What follows is our workflow for the general descriptive analysis of the Sanger sequencing data set for Zosterops. In this analysis we will describe the variation across individual Sanger sequenced loci and construct trees for each of these loci using distance-based and maximum likelihood methods.

title: Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees
text:
Getting started
We are using R version 4.5.2, RStudio version 2026.5.1.225 for the analysis. Quarto version 1.6.39 was used to document the workflow. Set the working directory in RStudio to one where the necessary phased Sanger sequencing alignments and other data are accessible.

title: Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees
text:
General methods summary

gDNA extraction
Whole genomic DNA (gDNA) was isolated from either blood or tissue samples using a magnetic bead based protocol (University of Kansas) (Rohland and Reich 2012) or standard phenol-chloroform-isoamyl alcohol (PCI) protocol followed by ethanol precipitation (Cincinnati Museum Center and Marshall University) and quantified by a Qubit dsDNA Assay.


PCR and Sanger sequencing
166 individual samples underwent polymerase chain reactions (PCRs) and Sanger sequencing across eight loci including two mtDNA and six nuclear protein-coding exons (nuDNA). Common sequence tags, either CS1 (5′-ACACTGACGACATGGTTCTACA) in the forward direction or CS2 (5′-TACGGTAGCAGAGACTTGGTCT) in the reverse direction, were added to all the oligonucleotide sequences in this study (Moonsamy et al. 2013). The addition of common 5′ tags allowed for CS1 and CS2 oligonucleotides to be utilized as sequencing primers for all amplicons across all loci. The NADH dehydrogenase subunit 2 (ND2) and cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1 (COI or COXI) were amplified using the primers L5216 and H6313 (Sorenson et al. 1999) and BIRDF1 and BIRDR2 (Hebert et al. 2004), respectively. Six nuDNA coding loci (B3GNT9, BIRC2, CCDC, GPRC6, LACTBL, and UBP38) were amplified using primers from Liu et al. (Liu et al. 2018). A complete list of the oligonucleotide sequences used as PCR primers in this study are shown below.

PCRs were performed in 10μL reactions in a 96-well thermal cycler (Life Technologies) with commercial polymerase master mixes (either Fidelitaq™ Master Mix, Affymetrix/USB or AmpliTaq Gold™ 360 Master Mix, Applied Biosystems™) and forward and reverse primers (0.5 μmol L−1 each; Integrated DNA Technology) using a thermal profile of 94°C for 4 min followed by 30 cycles of 1 min at 94°C, 1 min at 50°C, and 2 min at 72°C, and then a final extension cycle for 10 min at 72°C. The same thermal profile was utilized for all PCRs across all loci. Primers and excess dNTPs were inactivated with ExoSAP-IT™ (Applied Biosystems™) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Sequencing reactions were performed on ExoSAP-IT® treated PCR amplicons either in-house (Cincinnati Museum Center or Marshall University) using BigDye® v3.1 Cycle Sequencing and BigDye Xterminator® kits (Life Technologies) and separating on a 3130 Genetic Analyzer (Life Technologies) or by submitting for Sanger sequencing to Eurofins Genomics using their Prepaid Plate DNA kits. PCR amplicons were sequenced in both directions with primers based on the common sequence tags incorporated into all amplicons (CS1 and CS2).
Complementary strands were assembled and edited using either Geneious v8.1.4 or Geneious 8.1.9 (Biomatters, available from http://www.geneious.com) (Kearse et al. 2012). Chromatograms were inspected and every variation was checked for authenticity. The phase of nuclear alleles was determined statistically using Seqphase (Flot 2009) and Phase v2.1 (Stephens, Smith, and Donnelly 2001). Phased nuclear haplotypes and mitochondrial haplotypes were aligned using Geneious (Biomatters). General descriptive statistics for Sanger sequenced loci including nucleotide diversity, haplotype diversity, segregating sites, q, Tajima’s D (Tajima 1989), and the R2 test (Ramos-Onsins and Rozas 2002) as well as substitution model tests and trees and networks (distance-based and maximum likelihood) for individual loci were generated using the R packages ape (Paradis and Schliep 2019), pegas (Paradis 2010), and phangorn (Schliep 2011). R v4.4.2 was used throughout various analyses in this study (R Core Team, 2024).

title: Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees
text:
Data files
This dataset includes Sanger sequenced polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplicon alignments for two mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and six protein coding nuclear loci (nuDNA). Prior to this analysis Sanger sequencing ab1 files were uploaded to Geneious (Biomatters) for editing, alignment, and quality control. Multiple sequencing runs for each amplicon were assembled and assembled loci were aligned across individual samples using Geneious Alignment. Alignments for each locus were trimmed and edited in Geneious and the identity of each locus confirmed with a megablast search. The reading frame was set by eye by avoiding frames with stop codons and a blastp search was done on the translation consensus for each alignment to confirm the locus identity. Alignments were exported as fasta files and uploaded to the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GenBank (Sayers et al. 2024).
Alignments of diploid nuDNA loci were phased using PHASE 2.1.1 (Stephens, Smith, and Donnelly 2001). First, convert the alignment fasta files from Geneious to the inp format for PHASE 2.1.1 using the online SeqPHASE tool (Flot 2009). At the Genotypes to be phased prompt click the Browse button and select the appropriate fasta alignment. Click the Run SeqPHASE button. Once step 1 of the SeqPHASE process is completed retain the seqphase.const file in addition to the seqphase.inp file and rename each file appropriately to match the locus name (e.g., B3GNT9_seqphase.inp and B3GNT9_seqphase.const for locus B3GNT9).
Move the inp file from SeqPHASE to the directory with PHASE 2.1.1 and cd to that directory in the terminal. The inp file is used to run the following PHASE 2.1.1 command in the terminal. For each locus <numberseed> should be replaced with an arbitrary number selected by the user and LOCUSNAME replaced with the designated name for that particular locus. Because each locus is relatively short chose the S option at the modeling flag (-M) as it assumes no within-locus recombination. Additional parameters are explained in the documentation for PHASE 2.1.1 available here.
./PHASE -MS -d1 -S<numberseed> -p0.85 -q0.85 -x5 -X10 LOCUSNAME_seqphase.inp LOCUSNAME_seqphase.out 5000 2 500 
Further analysis will require fasta alignments for each locus where each diploid individual is associated with two sequences corresponding to each of the two phased alleles determined in PHASE 2.1.1. Return to the online SeqPHASE tool and click the link to step 2. Select the appropriate out file generated by the PHASE 2.1.1 run along with the matching const file generated from step 1 in the SeqPHASE tool. The Sort sequence box should be checked but the Reduce sequences box should not be checked. Click the Run SeqPHASE button and SeqPHASE will return a fasta file with the complete sequence alignment and two phased haplotypes designated by the project number for that individual sample followed by a and b respectively. Click the Click here to download the generated Fasta file link at the bottom of the page and rename the file to match the locus name. Including the const file and unchecking the Reduced sequences box will ensure the resulting fasta file includes the full length of the alignment, not just the variable sites.
The phasing procedure was repeated for each of the following nuDNA fasta alignments.

B3GNT9.fasta
BIRC2.fasta
CCDC.fasta
GPRC6.fasta
LACTBL.fasta
UBP38.fasta

Subsequent analysis requires the following phased nuDNA alignments from the procedures described above and the two mtDNA alignments (COI and ND2).

COI.fasta
ND2.fasta
B3GNT9_phased.fasta
BIRC2_phased.fasta
CCDC_phased.fasta
GPRC6_phased.fasta
LACTBL_phased.fasta
UBP38_phased.fasta

text:
Description of summary statistics and tree building procedure for a single locus

Packages
Begin the analysis by restarting the R session (Session/Restart R in RStudio), loading the initial package libraries, and starting a log of the analysis. Other package libraries will be loaded as needed in later blocks. The following R packages should be installed using the Tools/Install Packages feature in RStudio. The gt, dplyr, and webshot2 package libraries are used for creating a publication-quality summary table for all the loci.

logr (Bosak 2024) Optional if you wish to create a log file for the analysis.
ape (Paradis and Schliep 2019)
pegas (Paradis 2010)
phangorn (Schliep 2011)
gt (Iannone et al. 2024)
webshot2 (Chang 2025)
dplyr (Wickham et al. 2023)

Pairwise divergence
Determine the pairwise divergences among the sequences and display the 40 least divergent pairwise comparisons and the 40 greatest pairwise comparisons. Focusing on a particular pair of samples between Z. japonicus and Z. montanus (i.e., ZJal003a and ZMOvu001a) gives an idea of the mtDNA divergence within this focal group.

# Calculate pairwise divergences
pw_div_COI <- dist.dna(ZosteropsCOI, model = "raw")
# Convert the distance matrix to a data frame
pw_div_df_COI <- as.data.frame(as.matrix(pw_div_COI))
# Add row names as a column
pw_div_df_COI$Sequence <- rownames(pw_div_df_COI)
# Create a long format data frame
pw_div_long_format_COI <- data.frame(Sequence = rep(pw_div_df_COI$Sequence, each = nrow(pw_div_df_COI)),
                               Comparison = rep(pw_div_df_COI$Sequence, times = nrow(pw_div_df_COI)),
                               Divergence = as.vector(as.matrix(pw_div_COI)))
# Remove self-comparisons
pw_div_long_format_COI <- pw_div_long_format_COI[pw_div_long_format_COI$Sequence != pw_div_long_format_COI$Comparison, ]
# Find the least 40 divergences
pw_div_least_COI <- head(pw_div_long_format_COI[order(pw_div_long_format_COI$Divergence), ], 40)
# Find the greatest 40 divergences
pw_div_greatest_COI <- head(pw_div_long_format_COI[order(-pw_div_long_format_COI$Divergence), ], 40)
# Combine least and greatest divergences
pw_div_combined_results_COI <- rbind(pw_div_least_COI, pw_div_greatest_COI)
# View the results
print(pw_div_combined_results_COI)

Determine the pairwise divergences among the sequences and display the 40 least divergent pairwise comparisons and the 40 greatest pairwise comparisons.

# Calculate pairwise divergences
pw_div_ND2 <- dist.dna(ZosteropsND2, model = "raw")
# Convert the distance matrix to a data frame
pw_div_df_ND2 <- as.data.frame(as.matrix(pw_div_ND2))
# Add row names as a column
pw_div_df_ND2$Sequence <- rownames(pw_div_df_ND2)
# Create a long format data frame
pw_div_long_format_ND2 <- data.frame(Sequence = rep(pw_div_df_ND2$Sequence, each = nrow(pw_div_df_ND2)),
                                     Comparison = rep(pw_div_df_ND2$Sequence, times = nrow(pw_div_df_ND2)),
                                     Divergence = as.vector(as.matrix(pw_div_ND2)))
# Remove self-comparisons
pw_div_long_format_ND2 <- pw_div_long_format_ND2[pw_div_long_format_ND2$Sequence != pw_div_long_format_ND2$Comparison, ]
# Find the least 40 divergences
pw_div_least_ND2 <- head(pw_div_long_format_ND2[order(pw_div_long_format_ND2$Divergence), ], 40)
# Find the greatest 40 divergences
pw_div_greatest_ND2 <- head(pw_div_long_format_ND2[order(-pw_div_long_format_ND2$Divergence), ], 40)
# Combine least and greatest divergences
pw_div_combined_results_ND2 <- rbind(pw_div_least_ND2, pw_div_greatest_ND2)
# View the results
print(pw_div_combined_results_ND2)

# An index of segregating sites and number of segregating sites

# Total length of all sequences (number of sequences x sequence length)

# by the sequence length (calculation 1) and by extracting 
# the length value from the summary (caclulation 2)

NumberSequencesND21 <- lengthND2total/seqlengthND2
SummaryND2length <- unlist(strsplit(summaryND2[1,1], split = ":",

all.equal(NumberSequencesND21, NumberSequencesND22)

title: StarBEAST2
text: What follows is our workflow for the StarBEAST2 (Ogilvie, Bouckaert, and Drummond 2017) analysis for Zosterops. In this analysis we will generate Zosterops species trees from our individual Sanger sequenced loci using Bayesian phylogenetic inference and the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm.

title: StarBEAST2
text: What follows is our workflow for the StarBEAST2 (Ogilvie, Bouckaert, and Drummond 2017) analysis for Zosterops. In this analysis we will generate Zosterops species trees from our individual Sanger sequenced loci using Bayesian phylogenetic inference and the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm.

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Getting started
We are using BEAST v2.7.4 for the analysis (R. Bouckaert et al. 2019, 2014; Alexei J. Drummond et al. 2012; Alexei J. Drummond and Rambaut 2007). Quarto version 1.6.39 was used to document the workflow.

title: StarBEAST2
text:
General methods summary
A multilocus species tree was generated from the combined mtDNA and nuDNA Sanger sequencing data using StarBEAST2 (Ogilvie, Bouckaert, and Drummond 2017) implemented in BEAUTi2/BEAST2 v2.7.4 (Alexei J. Drummond et al. 2012; R. Bouckaert et al. 2014). We used bModelTest in StarBEAST2 to select the substitution model for each partition/locus (R. R. Bouckaert and Drummond 2017). A strict molecular clock approach was used for each locus. Priors for substitution rates were estimated based on lognormal distributions. The prior distribution for ND2 and COI was based on a mean of 0.0105 substitutions/site/lineage/Ma and a standard deviation of 1 (5–95% quantile range of 0.00123 - 0.033 and a median clock rate of 0.00637). This range is consistent with mtDNA substitution rates reported in birds (Fleischer, McIntosh, and Tarr 1998; Pereira and Baker 2006; Weir and Schluter 2008; Eo and DeWoody 2010). For the intron loci we based our prior substitution rate distributions on a mean 1/10th that of the ND2 and COI rates or 0.00105 substitutions/site/lineage/Ma and a standard deviation of 1 (5–95% quantile range is 0.000123 - 0.0033 and the median clock rate is 0.000637). We justified the substitution prior distribution for the nuclear loci on the basis of previous estimations of nuclear substitution rates in vertebrates relative to those of mtDNA (Johnson and Clayton 2000a, 2000b; Prychitko and Moore 2000; Armstrong, Braun, and Kimball 2001). Three analyses in StarBEAST2, labeled A, B, and C, were conducted with these parameters. The taxon set for the A and B runs included information on taxon (species and subspecies) and geography. The A runs included partitions for all eight loci and the B runs include only the mtDNA loci. Another set of runs (C runs) incorporated all partitions (mtDNA and nuDNA) but was based on only taxonomic assignments (genus, species, subspecies) for each sample and no additional geographic information. 20 independent runs were conducted for each analysis with 10M length Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains, 1M burnin lengths, and results stored every 20,000 iterations for each individual run. Log and tree files were combined across these 20 runs using LogCombiner and a maximum clade credibility consensus tree was generated using TreeAnnotator for each of the three analyses (both LogCombiner and TreeAnnotator are included in the BEAUTi2/BEAST2 v2.7.4 package).

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Data files
This analysis requires the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) alignments and the phased nuclear coding DNA (nuDNA) alignments from the Sanger sequenced loci. The protocol for phasing the nuDNA alignments may be found in the Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section. In addition a taxon set file will be required to assign individual samples to their taxon and/or population of origin.
Subsequent analysis requires the following fasta files including the mtDNA alignments and the phased nuDNA alignments from the procedure described in the Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section.

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Software and packages
BEAST2 software is available here. This analysis was conducted on a prior version of BEAST2 (v2.7.4 available here) but nearly identical results were achieved using the most recent version of BEAST2 (v2.7.7 as of the writing of this protocol). BEAUTi2 is the tool available with BEAST2 that allows for package management and a graphical user interface (GUI) to generate the xml files needed to run analyses. The programs LogCombiner and TreeAnnotator are also included with the BEAST2 install and will be needed to process the results of the MCMC runs. In addition, the program Tracer will be required to assess the results of an MCMC run and FigTree to edit and visualize species trees produced by BEAST2. Below is a summary of the needed software for this analysis and links to downloads.

BEAST2 v2.7.4 (R. Bouckaert et al. 2019) This install will include BEAST2, BEAUTi2, LogCombiner, and TreeAnnotator.
Tracer (Rambaut et al. 2018)
FigTree

In addition the following packages will need to be installed from the BEAUTi2 GUI using the package manager. To install packages in BEAUTi2 select File from the top bar and Manage Packages from the drop down menu. The package manager will display a table of installed packages and their latest versions. To install select the desired package and click on the Install/Upgrade button. After installing or upgrading packages you will have to close BEAUTi2 and restart before proceeding. Install the following packages.

bModelTest (R. R. Bouckaert and Drummond 2017)
StarBEAST2 (Ogilvie, Bouckaert, and Drummond 2017)

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Generating the xml file
After installing the needed packages restart BEAUTi2. From the File menu select Template and then StarBeast2. The StarBEAST2 template should display nine tabs titled as follows; Partitions, Taxon Sets, Tip Dates, Gene Ploidy, Population Model, Site Model, Clock Model, Priors, and MCMC.

Partitions
Sequence alignments will be added to the xml file in the Partitions tab. This can be done by either clicking the + button at the bottom of the tab and selecting Import Alignment from the subsequent menu options or by simply dragging the fasta file for each alignment into the Partitions tab. After specifying that an alignment is being imported select nucleotide when asked by BEAUTi2 to “Choose the datatype”. For each locus the correct number of taxa, sites, and data type should be listed. For each the file name will be used as the name BEAST2 uses for that particular locus. Also each locus should have a Site Model, Clock Model, and Tree unique to that alignment and with the same name. The Partition tab should look like this when completed.







Taxon sets
For the mtDNA alignments each individual sample has only a single sequence while there are two sequences for the diploid nuDNA alignments. The two phased sequences for each diploid individual sample should be labeled a and b (i.e. ZJja004a and ZJja004b are the two phased sequences for sample ZJja004). The a and b suffixes were automatically added to sample names for the phased sequences in PHASE 2.1.1 (see Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees). For consistency an a suffix was manually added to the sample name for each sequence in the mtDNA alignments to prevent a third sample name from appearing for each sample with both mtDNA and nuDNA sequences in the Taxon sets tab.
Some project numbers do not necessarily reflect the taxonomic origin of the individual samples. For example, samples ZJlo001 - ZJlo005 appear based on their project number designations to be Zosterops japonicus loochoensis but these project numbers were assigned in error before realizing they originated on the island of Chichijima outside the range of Z. japonicus loochoensis. For the Ogasawara Islands the subspecies designation for Z. japonicus is uncertain with some suspicion that these birds are subspecies hybrids between Z. japonicus stejnegeri in the Izu Islands and Z. japonicus alani in the Ogasawara/Volcano Islands. For our purposes we assigned birds in the Ogasawara and Volcano Islands the taxonomic designation Z. japonicus alani and birds in the Izu Islands Z. japonicus stejnegeri with the realization that gene flow may be occurring throughout these oceanic islands.
Click the Taxon sets tab. A list of sample names corresponding to the sequences in the alignments should appear in the Taxon column. For each sample a designation could be manually entered into the Species/Population column (time consuming) or automatically filled from a taxon sets file. To automatically add information on taxon assignment and/or population of origin click the Guess button at the bottom of the tab. Another window will open. Select the radio button corresponding to the read from file and the corresponding Browse button to select the appropriate taxon sets file. Click the Show options button and select txt to allow for the selection of txt files as taxon set entries. For the first set of BEAST2 runs samples were grouped by taxon (species and subspecies) and geography (island or island group) according to the Zosterops taxon sets A.txt file. Different sets of StarBEAST2 runs will employ different xml files each with a different taxon set. Below is what the Taxon sets tab should look like with Zosterops taxon sets A.txt. The first run will be with this taxon set specifying both taxon and geographic localities.







Tip dates
The next tab in BEAUTi2 is the Tip Dates tab. The only selection in this tab is a check box associated with Use tip dates. Leave this box unchecked and proceed to the next tab.







Gene ploidy
The ploidy for each locus is set on the next tab titled, appropriately, Gene Ploidy. A list of loci corresponding to those alignments imported into the Partitions tab should appear in the Gene Ploidy tab. Enter the ploidy for each locus in the corresponding box. nuDNA loci are diploid and biparentally inherited so for those loci enter a ploidy of 2.0. The mtDNA loci are uniparentally inherited and haploid. For the mtDNA loci enter 0.5 in the ploidy box. When completed this tab should appear as follows.







Population Model
In the Population Model tab select Analytical Population Size integration from the drop-down menu.







Site Model
Substitution models for each unlinked locus are set in the Site Model tab. For each locus use bModelTest to estimate the best substitution model. If the bModelTest package (see Software and Packages section above) was installed then this option should be available in BEAUTi2 in the drop-down at the top of the Site Model tab as the BEAST Model Test option. For each locus select BEAST Model Test from the drop-down and for Mutation Rate click the estimate box. Mutation rates among loci are estimated relative to one another so leave the Mutation Rate at 1.0 for each locus. Repeat this process for each locus.







Clock Model
Next set the molecular clock model. Click on the Clock Model tab. For each locus added to the Partition tab there should be a corresponding entry listed in the Clock Model tab. For all loci select Strict Clock from the drop-down menu at the top of the tab. The substitution rate for mtDNA was based on a divergence rate of 2.1% per million years (Ma). This equates to a mean of 1.05% or 0.0105 substitutions/site/lineage/Ma. This range is consistent with mtDNA substitution rates reported in birds (Fleischer, McIntosh, and Tarr 1998; Pereira and Baker 2006; Weir and Schluter 2008; Eo and DeWoody 2010). For both the mtDNA loci (COI and ND2) enter 0.0105 in the Clock.rate box and click the estimate box. For the nuDNA loci enter 0.00105 in the Clock.rate boxes and check the estimate box.







Priors
StarBEAST2 is a Bayesian method and as such it requires the user to set the priors for various parameters. For these analyses the default priors will be used for everything except for the clock rates. As we did for the Clock Model tab, clock rate priors will be based off of molecular clock rates estimated in the literature. Click on the Priors tab and scroll down to the strictClockRate values for each locus. Select the arrow symbol on the left to reveal the settings for the strictClockRate prior distribution for each locus. A LogNormal distribution from the drop down menu should be selected for all the strictClockRate priors. The box to the right should have the initial clock rate for each locus (same as defined in the Clock Rate tab) and show lower and upper bounds from 0.0 to infinity. Consistent with mtDNA substitution rates reported in birds (Fleischer, McIntosh, and Tarr 1998; Pereira and Baker 2006; Weir and Schluter 2008; Eo and DeWoody 2010) the mean clock rate (M) for the mtDNA loci (COI and ND2) will be set at 0.0105 substitutions/site/lineage/Ma with a standard deviation (S) of 1.0. Make sure the Mean in Real Space box is checked to view the prior distribution. For the mtDNA loci M = 0.0105 and S = 1.0 and a log normal distribution results in a 5 - 95% quantile range of 0.00123 - 0.033 and a median clock rate of 0.00637. The same conditions should be set for each nuDNA locus prior except that the mean (M) should be set at 1/10th the clock rate of the mtDNA loci (M = 0.00105). For the nuDNA loci the 5 - 95% quantile range is 0.000123 - 0.0033 and the median clock rate is 0.000637.







MCMC
The final tab (MCMC) sets the parameters for the run. Enter 10 million (10000000) in the Chain Length box. Enter 20000 in the box titled Store Every to indicate that results should be stored every 20,000 iteration of the MCMC chain. The burnin period should be 1 million. Enter 1000000 into the corresponding Pre Burnin box. The number of initiation attempts should be 10 (enter 10 for the Num Initiation Attempts box). Leave the remaining parameters at their default values.







Save xml file
All the needed parameters for the xml file are now completed. Save the file by selecting File from the top bar in BEAUTi2 and Save as.
Replicate multiple independent runs in three groups. Group A uses the Zosterops taxon sets A.txt file in the xml setup with both taxon and island information to define the individual samples. Group B also uses both taxon and island information in the BEAUTi2 Taxon sets tab during the xml setup but employs the Zosterops taxon sets mtDNA.txt file to define the individual samples. Group A xml files include all loci in the Partitions tab. Group B xml files include only the two mtDNA loci (COI and ND2) in the Partitions tab. Group C runs include all loci in the Partitions tab but use the Zosterops taxon sets B.txt file to define the samples by taxon only, collapsing populations across multiple localities into the same taxonomic group.
Create a working directory for each run labeled appropriately (A1-20; B1-20; C1-20). Create one xml file for each of these groups and duplicate that file 20 times changing the file name to create a sequential series of xml files from 1 -20 (A1-A20 for Group A, B1-B20 for Group B, and C1-C20 for group C).
Names for xml files for the first runs in each group are as follows. ‘STARBEAST274’ denotes the version of StarBEAST2 used and BMT denotes that these runs use bModelTest for the site model selection.

MCMC BEAST2 Runs
There will be three sets of 20 MCMC runs for this analysis. For each run follow these instructions. Create a separate directory for each run labeled A1 - A20 for the Group A runs, B1 - B20 for the Group B runs, and C1 - C20 for the Group C runs. Each directory should contain the appropriate xml file created in BEAUTi2. Open BEAST2. The following dialog window should appear. Use the Choose file… button to select the appropriate xml file for the run. A different value should appear in the Random number seed box with each separate run. If your machine will allow it, increase the number of threads and instances. Our runs were executed with 20 threads and 4 instances on either an Apple M1 iMac with 16GB RAM or an Apple M2 Max MacBook Pro with 96GB RAM. Click the Run button. Once BEAST2 is running the dialog window may be closed and the progress of the run monitored. Each run on either of these machines took approximately 30 - 40 minutes.

title: BPP and GDI based species delimitation
text: What follows is our workflow for the Bayesian Phylogenetics and Phylogeography (BP&P or hereafter just BPP) and genealogical diversity index (GDI) analyses for East Asian Zosterops. Using the multispecies coalescent (Flouri et al. 2019), the BPP software package v4.7.0 (Flouri et al. 2018), and the GDI heuristic species delimitation methods outlined in Leaché et al. (Leaché et al. 2018) this analysis attempts to estimate 𝜃 and test species hypotheses against the eight locus Sanger sequencing dataset for East Asian Zosterops (see Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section).

Using the multispecies coalescent (Flouri et al. 2019), the BPP software package v4.7.0 (Flouri et al. 2018), and the GDI heuristic species delimitation methods outlined in Leaché et al. (Leaché et al. 2018) this analysis attempts to estimate 𝜃 and test species hypotheses against the eight locus Sanger sequencing dataset for East Asian Zosterops (see Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section).

title: BPP and GDI based species delimitation
text:
Getting started
We are using R version 4.5.2 and RStudio version 2026.05.1 to illustrate the guide trees in for BPP, calculate GDI, and plot 𝜃 and GDI. Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow. The analysis was conducted using BPP v4.7.0. The BPP manual is an excellent introduction to these analyses.

title: BPP and GDI based species delimitation
text:
General methods summary
We tested hypotheses regarding species limits based on the eight locus Sanger sequencing dataset and the Bayesian Phylogenetic and Phylogeography (BP&P or hereafter BPP) program v4.7.0 (Yang 2015; Flouri et al. 2018) and estimates of the genealogical diversity index (GDI) (Jackson et al. 2016; Leaché et al. 2018). BPP allows for multiple analyses based on multilocus DNA alignments and the multispecies coalescent model including species delimitation from a fixed species tree (analysis A10 in BPP) and estimation of the population scaled mutation rate (𝛉 or q in BPP) and speciation or split times (𝜏 or t in BPP) from assigned species lineages on a fixed tree (analysis A00 in BPP).
We converted Sanger sequencing alignments, including both haploid mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) loci and phased diploid nuclear DNA (nuDNA) loci, into a single phylip formatted text file. A scalar file was used to set the heredity scalars to 0.25 for the mtDNA loci and 1 for the nuDNA loci. Four imap files were created to map individual samples to taxa on a fixed species tree. The ‘tip’ imap schema included five putative lineages; Z. japonicus, Z. meyeni, Z. montanus from the Northern Philippines, Z. montanus from the Southern Philippines and Indonesia, and Z. simplex. The ‘tip’ species tree was defined such that Z. japonicus, Z. meyeni, and the northern Z. montanus formed a single clade sister to the southern Z. montanus and within that clade Z. japonicus and Z. meyeni are sister. Z. simplex formed an outgroup to a clade with Z. japonicus. Z. meyeni, and both lineages of Z montanus. The ‘tip’ tree is plotted below.

library(ape)
ZOSTEROPSTREE <- read.tree(text = '((((Z. japonicus, Z. meyeni), Z. montanus NORTH), Z. montanus SOUTH), Z. simplex);')
plot(ZOSTEROPSTREE, edge.width = 4, label.offset = 0.1)








Three other imap files were constructed such that each pair of lineages was successively collapsed starting with Z. japonicus and Z. meyeni merged together (the ‘mid1’ tree), followed by the collapse of Z. japonicus, Z. meyeni, and the northern Z. montanus (the ‘mid2’ tree), and finally the collapse of Z. japonicus, Z. meyeni, and both Z. montanus lineages into a sister group to Z. simplex (the ‘root’ tree). Replicate BPP runs of the A00 analysis for each of these four fixed species trees provided estimates of 𝛉 and 𝜏 along each branch which could then be used to calculate GDI for each lineage. GDI is the complementary probability of \[e^{(-2\tau/\theta_A)}\]
and thus gives the probability of two sequences coalescing prior to (backwards in time) the divergence of population A and its sister lineage (Leaché et al. 2019) as follows.
\[GDI = 1 - e^{(-2\tau/\theta_A)}\]
Priors for the population 𝛉 and 𝜏 were based on an inverse G distribution defined by the parameters ⍺ and β. For all runs in BPP 𝛼 (a in BPP) was set at three and the 𝛽 (b in BPP) parameters for q (\(β_θ\) or bq) and t (\(β_τ\) or bt) varied among independent replicate runs. For the A10 runs various combinations of \(β_θ\) (0.001 – 0.1) and \(β_τ\) (0.0005 – 0.004) were used across runs corresponding to means of 0.0005 – 0.5 for 𝛉 and 0.00025 – 0.002 for 𝜏 prior distributions. These values were chosen based on what would be reasonable for a relatively recent set of lineages (< 1mya) and in consultation with the BPP manual. For all the A10 and A00 runs the GTR model was used with a burnin of 10,000 and a sample size of 100,000. Species delimitation algorithms 1 and 0 were tested in the A10 runs.
Three replicate runs were done for the A00 analyses for each of four combinations of prior parameters (\(β_θ\) and \(β_τ\)) across four fixed species trees (‘tip’, ‘mid1’, ‘mid2, and ‘root’) making a total of 48 A00 runs. Results from each set of three replicate runs under the same parameters were combined and GDI was calculated from estimates of 𝛉 and 𝜏. 𝛉 and GDI were plotted in R as density plots for each branch on the fixed species tree. This analysis was confined to those taxa with the greatest taxonomic uncertainty (Z. japonicus, Z. meyeni, and Z. montanus, with Z. simplex as an outgroup) and excluded all other taxa in this study (Z. erythropleurus, Z. everetti, Z. nigrorum, and Z. palpebrosus).

text:
Data files

Sequence alignments
The data used for this analysis will be restricted to those Sanger sequences from Zosterops japonicus, Z. meyeni, Z. montanus, and Z. simplex. The sequence file is in phylip format.
To illustrate the data format an excerpt of the sequence file ZosteropsBPP_JMMSseq.txt is shown below (ellipsis indicates where additional sequences from the original file have been left out). One alignment of individual sequences follows the other sequentially in a single file. A space followed by two numbers indicate the beginning of a locus. First is the number of individual sequences for that locus. Remember that for those loci from phased nuclear coding DNA (nuDNA) there will be two sequences for each individual with the individual identifying code followed by a and b to denote the two phased alleles (see Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section). The following number is the length of the sequence alignment in base pairs (bp). Each sequence will lead with the sample, an a for the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) loci or either a or b for the phased nuDNA loci, and underscore, the locus name (e.g., COI, ND2, B3GNT9), a ^ symbol, and finally the individual sample name (minus the allelic designations, a and/or b). The individual sample name following the ^ symbol should match the individual names used to map taxon names (i.e., the imap file).

The heredity file ZosteropsBPP_heredity.txt below defines the heredity scalars for each locus. Mitochondrial loci have the scalar 0.25 and biparentally inherited nuclear loci have the scalar of 1.0. The scalars in the heredity file are in the the same order as the mtDNA and nuDNA alignments in the sequences file with the two mtDNA loci (COI and ND2) appearing first. Taxon maps and guide trees
The final data file needed for these analyses is an imap file saved in txt format that maps the taxon and/or population designations to individual samples. Individual samples in the imap file should match those in the phylip formatted sequence file. Four imap files will be needed for the analysis.

ZosteropsBPPtip_imap.txt
ZosteropsBPPmid1_imap.txt
ZosteropsBPPmid2_imap.txt
ZosteropsBPProot_imap.txt

Codes in these files are designated for each taxon as follows.

Jp - Z. japonicus
Me - Z. meyeni
MoN - Z. montanus Northern Philippines including subspecies halconensis (Mindoro) and whiteheadi (Luzon)
MoS - Z. montanus Southern Philippines, Palawan, and Indonesia including subspecies Z. montanus diuatae (Mindanao), Z. montanus vulcani (Mindanao), Z. montanus pectoralis (Negros), Z. montanus parkesi (Palawan), Z. montanus montanus (Indonesia), and an unnamed Z. montanus population on the Philippine island of Panay.
Si - Z. simplex including populations on the island of Taiwan and Mainland Asia.



Trees

TIP tree
This topology is derived from the single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) dataset analyzed in the Singular Value Decomposition Quartets (SVDQ) package (see Species trees and delimitation with SVDQuartets, PICL, and DELINEATE section) and the Sanger sequencing dataset analyzed in BEAST2 (see Star BEAST2 section). Branches are color coded here to match the corresponding density distributions in subsequent analyses. Each tree collapses taxa so BPP analyses may estimate 𝜃 (q) and 𝜏 (t) along each branch.

TIP <- read.tree(text = '((((Jp,Me),MoN),MoS),Si);')
edge_colors <- c("#EEA2AD", "#1E90FF", "#FF8C00", "#D82632", 
                 "#FED439", "#B66DFF", "#FA9C88", "#008600")
plot(TIP, edge.color = edge_colors[1:length(TIP$edge)], 
     edge.width = 4, label.offset = 0.1)
nodes <- c("A", "B", "C", "D")
nodelabels(nodes)
edgelabels()










MID1 tree
Collapses the Z. japonicus and Z. meyeni branches.

MID1 <- read.tree(text = '(((JpMe,MoN),MoS),Si);')
plot(MID1, edge.width = 4, label.offset = 0.1)










MID2 tree
Collapses the Z. japonicus/Z. meyeni branch and Z. montanus from the Northern Philippines.

MID2 <- read.tree(text = '((JpMeMoN,MoS),Si);')
plot(MID2, edge.width = 4, label.offset = 0.1)










ROOT tree
Collapses Z. japonicus, Z. meyeni, Z. motanus in the Northern Philippines, and Z. montanus in Indonesia and the Southern Philippines into a single branch connected to the outgroup (Z. simplex) by a single node.

ROOT <- read.tree(text = '(JpMeMoNMoS,Si);')
plot(ROOT, edge.width = 4, label.offset = 0.1)

title: BPP and GDI based species delimitation
text:
BPP control files
Control files were created to run BPP analyses across a variety of models and prior distributions.

BPP A10 control files
The BPP analyses designated the A runs conduct a species delimitation analysis on a fixed species tree. The species tree used for the A10 runs is the TIP tree with each taxon as a separate branch (Z. japonicus, Z. meyeni, Z. montanus from the Northern Philippines, Z. montanus from the Southern Philippines and Indonesia, and Z. simplex, see [Trees]). Below is the ctl file for the first A series BPP run (A1). Several parameters on the control (ctl) files are edited to execute different runs including the \(β_θ\) and \(β_τ\) parameters for the inverse 𝛤 prior distribution, and the species delimitation model (0 or 1). The \(β_θ\) and \(β_τ\) parameters for the inverse 𝛤 prior distribution are edited at the thetaprior and tauprior lines, each of which is specified by two digits for 𝛼 (a) and 𝛽 (b), but only the 𝛽 value will be changed across runs. A list of the ctl files and the key parameters for each A series run are shown in the [BPP A10 runs] table in the [A10 results] section below. Note that beginning a line in the ctl file with an asterisk causes BPP to ignore that line. Adding and deleting asterisks in front of particular lines of commands is a convenient way to add or delete particular parameters.
seed =  -1
seqfile = ZosteropsBPP_JMMSseq.txt
Imapfile = ZosteropsBPPtip_imap.txt
outfile = ZosteropsBPP_A10_RUNA1.out.txt
mcmcfile = ZosteropsBPP_A10_RUNA1.mcmc.txt

* speciesdelimitation = 0 # fixed species tree
* speciesdelimitation = 1 0 2    # speciesdelimitation algorithm0 and finetune(e)
speciesdelimitation = 1 1 2 1 # speciesdelimitation algorithm1 finetune (a m)
speciestree = 0 0.4 0.2 0.1   # speciestree pSlider ExpandRatio ShrinkRatio

* speciesmodelprior = 1  # 0: uniform LH; 1:uniform rooted trees; 2: uniformSLH; 3: uniformSRooted

species&tree = 5  Jp Me MoN MoS Si
                  93 10 6 25 14
                 ((((Jp, Me), MoN), MoS), Si);
phase = 0    # 0: phased sequences, 1: unphased diploid sequences, in newest version this command is called phase
usedata = 1    # 0: no data (prior); 1:seq like
nloci = 8    # number of data sets in seqfile
model = gtr
alphaprior = 1 1 4
cleandata = 1    # remove sites with ambiguity data (1:yes, 0:no)?

thetaprior = 3 0.01 e  # invgamma(a, b) for theta
tauprior = 3 0.002  # invgamma(a, b) for root tau & Dirichlet(a) for other tau's

locusrate = 1 0 0 1 iid   # (0: No variation, 1: estimate, 2: from file)
heredity = 2 ZosteropsBPP_heredity.txt   # (0: No variation, 1: estimate, 2: from file) & a_gamma b_gamma (if 1)
threads = 8
    
finetune = 1: 8 0.01 0.001 0.01 0.01  # auto (0 or 1): MCMC step lengths, last two values are for lrht and phi which in this run are not estimated so those numbers are excluded, if I wanted to add those estimates I would need two additional finetune values

print = 1 1 0 0   # MCMC samples, locusrate, heredityscalars Genetrees
burnin = 10000
sampfreq = 2
nsample = 100000


BPP A00 control files
The BPP analyses designated the B, C, D, and E runs work from a fixed species tree without the BPP species delimitation analysis. For the B runs the \(β_θ\) and \(β_τ\) parameters for the inverse 𝛤 prior distribution are 0.001 and 0.004 respectively. For the C runs the \(β_θ\) and \(β_τ\) parameters are 0.002 and 0.004, for the D runs these values are 0.001 and 0.0005, and for the E runs these values are 0.002 and 0.0005. Running BPP independently for different, but reasonable, distributions of 𝜃 and 𝜏 is used to assess the sensitivity of our estimates to the priors. Note that for all the A00 runs (run series B-E) the speciesdelimitation selections are omitted by being preceded by an asterisk, as is the speciesmodelprior selection. Three replicate runs are done for each combination of 𝜃 and 𝜏 priors and each species tree (TIP, MID1, MID2, and ROOT, see above). Starting each ctl file with seed = -1 creates a different random number seed for each replicate run. Independent runs for each species tree will be used to estimate 𝜃 and 𝜏 which will in turn be used to estimate the GDI for each branch (see [Genealogical diversity index (GDI)]). Below is an example of a B run control file. A list of the ctl files and the key parameters for each set of runs in the B-E series run are shown in the [BPP A00 runs] table in the [A00 GDI results] section below.
seed =  -1
seqfile = ZosteropsBPP_JMMSseq.txt
Imapfile = ZosteropsBPPtip_imap.txt
outfile = ZosteropsBPP_A00_RUNB1.out.txt
mcmcfile = ZosteropsBPP_A00_RUNB1.mcmc.txt

speciesdelimitation = 0 # fixed species tree
* speciesdelimitation = 1 0 2    # speciesdelimitation algorithm0 and finetune(e)
* speciesdelimitation = 1 1 2 1 # speciesdelimitation algorithm1 finetune (a m)
speciestree = 0 0.4 0.2 0.1   # speciestree pSlider ExpandRatio ShrinkRatio

* speciesmodelprior = 1  # 0: uniform LH; 1:uniform rooted trees; 2: uniformSLH; 3: uniformSRooted

species&tree = 5  Jp Me MoN MoS Si
                  93 10 6 25 14
                 ((((Jp, Me), MoN), MoS), Si);
phase = 0    # 0: phased sequences, 1: unphased diploid sequences, in newest version this command is called phase
usedata = 1    # 0: no data (prior); 1:seq like
nloci = 8    # number of data sets in seqfile
model = gtr
alphaprior = 1 1 4
cleandata = 1    # remove sites with ambiguity data (1:yes, 0:no)?

thetaprior = 3 0.001 e  # invgamma(a, b) for theta
tauprior = 3 0.004  # invgamma(a, b) for root tau & Dirichlet(a) for other tau's

locusrate = 1 0 0 1 iid   # (0: No variation, 1: estimate, 2: from file)
heredity = 2 ZosteropsBPP_heredity.txt   # (0: No variation, 1: estimate, 2: from file) & a_gamma b_gamma (if 1)
threads = 8
    
finetune = 1: 8 0.01 0.001 0.01 0.01  # auto (0 or 1): MCMC step lengths, last two values are for lrht and phi which in this run are not estimated so those numbers are excluded, if I wanted to add those estimates I would need two additional finetune values

print = 1 1 0 0   # MCMC samples, locusrate, heredityscalars Genetrees
burnin = 10000
sampfreq = 2
nsample = 100000

title: BPP and GDI based species delimitation
text:
Genealogical diversity index (GDI)
\(2\tau/\theta_A\) is the population divergence time for population \(A\) in coalescent units. One coalescent unit is equal to \(2N_A\) generations where \(N_A\) is the effective population size of \(A\). \(e^{(-2\tau/\theta_A)}\) is the probability that two sequences (\(a_1\) and \(a_2\)) from population \(A\) fail to coalesce before the divergence (𝜏) of \(A\) from its sister lineage. The GDI is the complementary probability of \(e^{(-2\tau/\theta_A)}\) and reflects the probability that \(a_1\) and \(a_2\) coalesce prior to (going backwards in time) the divergence between population \(A\) and its sister lineage. GDI therefore may be calculated from 𝜃 and 𝜏 using the following equation (Jackson et al. 2016; Leaché et al. 2018).
\[GDI = 1 - e^{(-2\tau/\theta_A)}\]
The BPP A00 analyses will estimate 𝜃 and 𝜏 along each branch in a given tree and we then use those values to calculate the GDI for each branch.

title: BPP and GDI based species delimitation
text:
Running BPP
Upon installing BPP v4.7.0 a directory will be created containing a bin folder with the BPP application (on Mac OS that directory is bpp-4.7.0-macos-aarch64). To execute a BPP run copy the following needed files to this directory (in this example we will be running the B1 run, an A00 analysis with ctl file ZosteropsA00_RUNB1.bpp.ctl).

ZosteropsA00_RUNB1.bpp.ctl
ZosteropsBPP_JMMSseq.txt
ZosteropsBPP_heredity.txt
ZosteropsBPPtip_imap.txt

The only files that change between runs is the ctl file and the imap file.
Navigate to the BPP directory with the bin folder containing the BPP program.
In the terminal run the following command (make sure the needed files are in the working directory).
bin/bpp --cfile ZosteropsA00_RUNB1.bpp.ctl
Upon completion multiple files will be generated by this analysis.

FigTree.tre This is a tree file generated with 𝜃, 𝜏, and 95% highest posterior density (HPD) for 𝜏 as branch lengths based on the tree topology given in the analysis.
Eight sample.txt files, one for each locus in the sequence file (locus.[1-8].sample.txt).
SeedUsed A text file recording the random number seed used for the run.
ZosteropsBPP_A00_RUNB1.mcmc.txt A text file containing the results from the MCMC chain.
ZosteropsBPP_A00_RUNB1.out.txt A text file summarizing the output of the run (for A10 runs this will include whether the analysis supported a split at each node along with the posterior probability of a split). For each run the name of the mcmc and out files will be specified by the ctl file.

Repeat this process for each ctl file and for the A00 runs replicate each run three times. Once each run is complete, copy and organize the results to an appropriate directory.

A10 species delimitation results
In the A10 species delimitation analysis BPP returns a posterior probability for each node in the species tree provided, for this analysis the TIP tree in the file ZosteropsBPPtip_imap.txt. A result of 1 indicates a split at that node was supported and a 0 indicates that a lump was supported for the branches at that node. For all the A10 runs listed in the [BPP A10 runs] table above a split was supported at every node (1111, see tree below) with a posterior probability of 1.0.

# A RUNS are BPP runs under the A10 conditions with species delimitation 
# under a fixed tree.
# B-E RUNS are BPP runs under the A00 conditions with no 
# species delimitation and a fixed tree.
# Each set of runs are done under three replicates, four imap files 
# corresponding to different branches of the tree (tip, mid1, mid2, root), 
# and four different combinations of theta and tau prior distributions.
# Taxon codes for trees: Jp (Z. japonicus), Me (Z. meyeni), 
# MoN (Northern Philippine Z. montanus on Luzon and Mindoro), 
# MoS (Southern Philippine Z. montanus in the Visayas and Mindanao), 
# Si (outgroup, Z. simplex on Mainland Asia and Taiwan)
# Trees for .ctl files...
# B RUNS Tip ((((Jp, Me), MoN), MoS), Si)
# C RUNS Mid1 (((JpMe, MoN), MoS), Si)
# D RUNS Mid2 ((JpMeMoN, MoS), Si)
# E RUNS Root (JpMeMoNMoS, Si)
# Beta values for Theta and Tau...

# Tip B1-3 0.001 0.004 B4-6 0.002 0.004 B7-9 0.001 0.0005 B10-12 0.002 0.0005

title: Distance trees, PCA, UMAP, and DAPC analyses
text: What follows is an analysis of the Zosterops single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data from our double digest restriction-site associated DNA (ddRAD) library or RADseq. This analysis seeks to describe general metrics of diversity and variation in East Asian Zosterops and makes some attempt to assess the utility of these data in clustering individuals by putative taxonomic and population groups.

title: Distance trees, PCA, UMAP, and DAPC analyses
text:
Getting started
We are using R version 4.5.2, RStudio version 2026.05.1 for the analysis. Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow. Set the working directory in RStudio to one where the vcf.gz zipped data file and a txt file denoting the identity of the samples are accessible.

title: Distance trees, PCA, UMAP, and DAPC analyses
text:
General methods summary

RADseq-derived SNP dataset
The RADseq-derived SNP dataset in this study was previously analyzed in DeRaad et al. (D. A. DeRaad et al. 2024), which includes detailed methodological description. Briefly, restriction site associated DNA libraries were constructed by digesting gDNA using the enzyme NdeI and performing size selection for fragments between 495 – 605 base-pairs (bp). The complete library preparation protocol is available at https://github.com/DevonDeRaad/zosterops.rad/blob/main/lab.protocols/MSG-NdeI_2plates-150samples_DAD-Moyle_230530.doc. Pooled, bar-coded libraries were sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq2000 at the University of Kansas Genomic Sequencing Core using a P2 flow cell to generate 414,215,817 single-end 100 bp reads (approximately 41Gb raw sequence data). Raw genomic sequencing data is publicly available via the SRA BioProject PRJNA1079333 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra/PRJNA1079333).


Read mapping, variant calls, and filtering
Mapping, variant calling, and filtering was performed as in DeRaad et al. (2023) and DeRaad et al. (2024) (D. A. DeRaad et al. 2023, 2024). Raw data was demultiplexed and reads of low quality and with uncalled bases were removed using Stacks v2.41 (Rochette, Rivera-Colón, and Catchen 2019). Reads were then mapped to a publicly available Z. japonicus genome assembly available at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/assembly/GCA_017612475.1 (Venkatraman, Fleischer, and Tsuchiya 2021) using the Burrows-Wheeler Alignment tool (BWA) v0.7.17 (Li and Durbin 2009). SAMtools v1.3.1 (Li et al. 2009) was used to convert files to a sorted bam format and RAD loci were identified in Stacks using the ‘gstacks’ module and exported as a variant call format (VCF) file resulting in an unfiltered SNP dataset containing 236,767 SNPs shared among 155 individual samples with 65.5% missing genotypes. The R packages vcfR v1.14.0 (Knaus and Grünwald 2017) and SNPfiltR v1.0.1 (D. DeRaad 2023) were used to visualize parameter distributions and filter the SNP data for quality. The final filtered VCF file included 15,704 SNPs across 124 individual samples with 5.3% missing data. A more detailed description of the filtering protocol may be found in DeRaad et al. (D. A. DeRaad et al. 2024) and at: https://devonderaad.github.io/zosterops.rad/zost.radseq.filtering.html.
A pairwise distance matrix based on Nei’s D (Nei 1972) was generated from the filtered SNP dataset using the R package StAMPP v1.6.3 (Pembleton, Cogan, and Forster 2013) and used to construct a neighbor-net phylogenetic network using the R package SplitsTree4 v4.15.1 (Huson and Bryant 2005). This allowed us to visualize the data and, in some cases, validate the identity of individual samples for subsequent analyses. For example, the sample designated Zsim30897 was initially identified as Z. simplex, and given an identification code to match, however in a phylogenetic network this sample clustered with the very divergent Z. palpebrosus and was therefore revised to match that identity. Associated R code and the phylogenetic network from SplitsTree v4.15.1 are described in DeRaad et al. (D. A. DeRaad et al. 2024) and may be viewed at https://devonderaad.github.io/zosterops.rad/splitstree.html.


General SNP visualization and multivariate analyses
Various approaches were employed to visualize variation in the SNP dataset. The filtered SNP VCF file was converted to a genlight object for subsequent analyses using the ‘vcfR2genlight’ command in the R package vcfR (Knaus and Grünwald 2017). The R package Poppr (Kamvar, Tabima, and Grünwald 2014) was used to generate a minimum spanning network (MSN) and a distance tree based on the unweighted pair group method (UPGMA). Bootstrapping was performed for the UPGMA tree with 100 replicates.
A principal component analysis (PCA) and a discriminant function analysis of principal components (DAPC) was conducted using the R package adegenet (T. Jombart 2008) following the methodology from Jombart et al. (Thibaut Jombart, Devillard, and Balloux 2010). DAPC is a multivariate method that takes principal components (PCs) and partitions variance into within- and among-group components in a way that maximizes discrimination among the groups. DAPC makes no explicit assumptions regarding recombination or panmixia. This allows use of the full SNP dataset without additional filtering to reduce the likelihood of linkage as is required for other clustering analyses such as Structure (Pritchard, Stephens, and Donnelly 2000; Porras-Hurtado et al. 2013) or Admixture (Alexander, Novembre, and Lange 2009).
The DAPC analysis was conducted in R and based from a tutorial available at https://grunwaldlab.github.io/Population_Genetics_in_R/DAPC.html. Samples were grouped by a combination of species, subspecies, and geography with Z. japonicus split into the most far-flung Z. japonicus alani subspecies in the Ogasawara and Volcano Islands and a broader Z. japonicus group encompassing the remaining subspecies. Z. montanus samples were grouped into a Northern Philippine group including Z. montanus whiteheadi on Luzon and Z. montanus halconensis on Mindoro, Z. montanus parkesi on Palawan, and a southern group including the remaining Z. montanus subspecies from the Visayas, Camiguin South, Mindanao, Sulawesi, and Java. The remaining samples were assigned to groups based on their species.
PCA was conducted on the filtered SNP dataset (15,704 SNPs, 124 individual samples) using the sample groups described above. PCs were generated using the ‘glPca’ function in adegenet (T. Jombart 2008). We generated plots in two dimensions (PCs 1-2) and in three dimensions (PCs 1-3) using the R package plotly (Sievert 2020).  
We conducted a cross-validation analysis to help determine the optimal number of PCs to be retained in the DAPC by examining the proportion of successful assignments for each PC for the first 50 PCs and 100 replicate runs per PC. This analysis showed that successful assignments greatly increased from PC1 to PC13 and leveled off until declining at approximately PC30. We also estimated the difference between the proportion of successful reassignments using the real groups and assignments of individual samples into randomly assigned groups (i.e. the a-score). The mean a-score across replicate runs therefore estimates the average percent improvement in discrimination over that based on random groupings. We used the ‘dapc’ function in adegenet to estimate the mean a-score across 30 replicate runs and for each of the first 40 PCs. This process was repeated 100 times generating an optimization graph for each run. The median optimal number of PCs was calculated from these 100 runs and used in the subsequent DAPC analysis. The DAPC analysis was conducted based on the optimal number of PCs, determined as described above, in which we estimated the posterior membership probability for each individual sample. We conducted two additional DAPC analyses based on 50% fewer and 50% greater than the optimal number of PCs.
In addition to PCA we conducted a second dimensionality reduction on the SNP data using the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) method (“Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection” 2024). Analysis via both methods allowed for the visualization of the SNP data by a linear method emphasizing variation (PCA) and a non-linear method emphasizing global structure among groups (UMAP). UMAP was performed with the ‘umap’ function in the R package umap (Konopka 2023) and plots generated in two and three dimensions using the R package plotly (Sievert 2020).

text:
Minimum spanning network (MSN)
Create a minimum spanning network (MSN). Export the figure as either a pdf or png file using the export function in RStudio. Beginning here we will set a different random seed for each operation where a seed is required. Setting inds to some set of characters not in the dataset (in this instance just a blank space) and nodelab to some arbitrarily large number in plot_poppr_msn will leave blank points on the network. Removing these arguments will result in each point on the network labeled with the corresponding sample name.

MSNseed = sample(1:999, 1)
print(MSNseed)

set.seed(MSNseed)

Conduct a principal component analysis (PCA) on the gl.ZosteropsSNPs object. Graph the percent of variance explained by each principal component (PC) and create two PC plots; one plot with PC1 and PC2 and a three-dimensional plot with PC1, PC2, and PC3.

Calculate the centroids for each group based on the first three principal components and the pairwise Euclidean distances between each pair of groups.

Zosterops_PCAscores <- ZosteropsSNPsPCA$scores[, 1:3]
Zosterops_PCAgroups <- gl.ZosteropsSNPs@pop
Zosterops_PCAdf <- data.frame(Zosterops_PCAscores, Group = Zosterops_PCAgroups)
Zosterops_unique_PCAgroups <- unique(Zosterops_PCAgroups)
Zosterops_PCAcentroids <- data.frame(Group = character(), PC1 = numeric(), PC2 = numeric(), PC3 = numeric(), PC4 = numeric(), PC5 = numeric(), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# Loop through each unique group to calculate centroids
for (group in Zosterops_unique_PCAgroups) {
  group_scores <- Zosterops_PCAdf[Zosterops_PCAdf$Group == group, 1:3]
  centroid <- colMeans(group_scores, na.rm = TRUE)
  Zosterops_PCAcentroids <- rbind(Zosterops_PCAcentroids, 
                                   data.frame(Group = group, 
                                              PC1 = centroid[1], 
                                              PC2 = centroid[2], 
                                              PC3 = centroid[3]))
}

title: Distance trees, PCA, UMAP, and DAPC analyses
text:
Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP)
Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) (“Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection” 2024) is a non-linear, stochastic algorithm to reduce dimensionality for visualization of multivariate data. UMAP seeks to preserve as much of the relationships among groups in the dataset as possible while reducing to a minimal number of components. In this case we are visualizing the SNP data with UMAP for two and three dimensions using the umap package and plotting the results for each analysis using the plot_ly command from the plotly package. The n_neighbors, min_dist, and metric arguments all reflect the default values. For each plot save as html files using the saveWidget command in the htmlwidgets package.

# Set random seed
UMAPseed = sample(1:999, 1)
print(UMAPseed)

[1] 733

set.seed(UMAPseed)

ZosteropsUMAP_df <- as.data.frame(ZosteropsUMAP_results$layout)

title: Distance trees, PCA, UMAP, and DAPC analyses
text:
Discriminant analysis of principal components (DAPC)

DAPC cross-validation, a-scores, and optimal number of PCs for discrimination
Discriminant analysis of principal components (DAPC) is a multivariate method that takes principal components (PCs) and partitions variance into within- and among-group components in a way that maximizes discrimination among the groups (Thibaut Jombart, Devillard, and Balloux 2010). DAPC makes no explicit assumptions regarding recombination or panmixia. This allows use of the full SNP dataset without worrying about filtering to reduce the likelihood of linkage as is required for STRUCTURE or ADMIXTURE. A tutorial on DAPC is available here. First conduct a cross-validation analysis to help determine the optimal number of PCs to be retained in the DAPC. Test between 1 and 50 PCs (n.pca = 1:50) with 100 replicate runs per PC (n.rep = 100) of the cross-validation analysis. Use the multicore option and 6 CPUs (ncpus = 6L), or potentially more if your machine allows it. Even running multiple cores this run can take a while to execute. Executing this analysis within the system.time command will return an elapsed time for the operation. This will return a graph showing the proportion of successful group predictions on the y-axis and the results from the individual replicate runs for each PC on the x-axis.

a-scores
The DAPC cross validation provides some clues as to where we no longer need to add PCs to the DAPC to get increased discrimination, but we want to know exactly how many PCs is optimum for discrimination. The a-score is the difference between the proportion of successful reassignments using the real groups and assignments into randomly assigned groups. Thus the average a-score is the average percent improvement in discrimination over that based on random groupings. The code below will estimate the a-score across 30 replicate runs (n.sim = 30) and 40 PCs (n.pca = 40) showing the result per group for each run, the average across all replicates per group, and the overall average.

ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_OPTIMUM <- dapc(gl.ZosteropsSNPs, n.pca = 40, n.da = nPop(gl.ZosteropsSNPs)-1)
a.score(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_OPTIMUM, n.pca = 1:ncol(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_OPTIMUM$tab), n=30, plot = FALSE, n.sim = 30)

DAPC scatter plots and bar graphs
Conduct the final DAPC analysis with group assignments for each individual sample. Three runs will be repeated for this analysis. One of those runs uses the optimal number of PCs from the prior iterated a-score estimations (the median optimal number of PCs across 100 replicate runs of the optimal a-score estimation). The other two runs of the DAPC analysis are four PCs less than the optimal and four PCs greater than the optimal number of PCs. Generate a scatter plot from the DAPC analysis and a bar plot showing the probability of assignment for each individual sample. Save both the scatter plot and bar graphs as pdf files and generate a tab-delimited table of the results for each individual sample with the columns being the original assigned population, the sample, the population assigned by the DAPC, and the posterior probability of that particular assignment. In addition, for each replicate run generate a loading plot displaying how each SNP contributes to the PCs for the optimal number of PCs and four less than and four greater than the optimal number. Export each loading plot as a pdf.

n.pca.values <- c(4, 8, 12)
for (n.pca in n.pca.values) {
  DAPCseed = sample(1:999, 1)
  print(DAPCseed)
  set.seed(DAPCseed)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPC <- dapc(gl.ZosteropsSNPs, n.pca = n.pca, n.da = nPop(gl.ZosteropsSNPs)-1)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_contributions <- loadingplot(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC$var.contr, axis = 2, thres = 0.0025, lab.jitter = 1)
  DAPCscatter <- scatter(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC, col = ColorPal_CUSTOM, cex = 3, legend = TRUE, clabel = F, posi.leg = "bottomleft", scree.pca = TRUE,
          posi.pca = "topright", cleg = 0.75)
  DAPCscatter
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults <- as.data.frame(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC$posterior)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults$pop <- pop(gl.ZosteropsSNPs)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults$indNames <- rownames(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults <- pivot_longer(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, -c(pop, indNames))
  head(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, n = 11)
  nPCAtitle <- paste(n.pca, "principal components")
  print(nPCAtitle)
  colnames(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults) <- c("Original_Pop","Sample","Assigned_Pop","Posterior_membership_probability")
  DAPCbar <- ggplot(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, aes(x=Sample, y=Posterior_membership_probability, fill=Assigned_Pop))
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + geom_bar(stat='identity') 
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + ggtitle(nPCAtitle)
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + scale_fill_manual(values = ColorPal_CUSTOM) 
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + facet_grid(~Original_Pop, scales = "free")
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size = 8))
  print(DAPCbar)
  write.table(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, file = paste("ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults","_",n.pca,"PCs.txt"), row.names = FALSE, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE)
}
